title: Cheapest Way to Level Every Value
statement:
You get two arrays of the same length, nums and cost. You may raise or lower any nums[i] by 1 as many times as you like, and each such step on index i costs cost[i].

Return the smallest total cost to make all values in nums equal. The common value can be any integer you choose.

examples.why: Level everything to 9: 8 · 1 + 5 · 1 = 13. The plain median 4 costs 3 + 0 + 5 · 5 = 28, because moving the 9 is expensive.
Weight 4 sits at 2 and weight 4 at 6, so every target from 2 to 6 costs the same 16.

hints: Write the total cost as a function of the target value x. What does its graph look like as x moves from the smallest value to the largest?
Each term cost[i] · |nums[i] − x| is a V shape, and a sum of V shapes is convex: it goes down, then up. So you can binary search on x by comparing f(x) with f(x + 1).
Faster still: moving x one step right costs the weight on the left and saves the weight on the right. The best x is where the weight to its left first reaches half the total: the weighted median.

explain.intuition:
Fix a target x. The cost is f(x) = Σ cost[i] · |nums[i] − x|. Each term is a V with its tip at nums[i], and adding V shapes gives a bowl: f falls, flattens, then rises. Any bowl-shaped function can be minimized by binary search: if f(mid) < f(mid + 1), the bottom is at or left of mid; otherwise it is to the right.

The slope tells you exactly where the bottom is. Moving x one step right makes every value on the left one step more expensive and every value on the right one step cheaper. So keep moving right while the weight on the right is bigger than the weight on the left. That stops at the weighted median: sort by value and walk until the running cost weight reaches half of the total. It is the median where each value counts cost[i] times, which is why the heavy 9 in the first example wins.
steps: Pair each value with its cost and sort the pairs by value.
Compute the total weight W = Σ cost.
Walk the sorted pairs, adding weights, and stop at the first value where the running weight times 2 is at least W. That value is the target.
pitfalls: Using the plain median or the average. Both ignore the costs; the first example shows the plain median costing 28 instead of 13.
Binary searching by comparing f(mid) to f(lo) or f(hi). On a flat bottom that can step the wrong way; compare neighbours f(mid) and f(mid + 1).
Overflow in languages with 32-bit integers. The answer can reach about 10¹⁴ here, so use 64-bit sums.

solutions.title: Try every value as the target
solutions.idea: The best target is always one of the existing values (the bottom of a sum of V shapes sits at a tip). Try each one.

solutions.title: Binary search on the target
solutions.idea: f(x) is convex. Compare f(mid) with f(mid + 1) to decide which half holds the bottom.

solutions.title: Weighted median
solutions.idea: Sort by value and stop where the running weight reaches half of the total. Moving away from that point in either direction can only cost more.

followups: Each step up costs up[i] and each step down costs down[i], with different prices. Is the cost still convex, and how does the median rule change?
Values arrive one at a time and you must report the best cost after each. Which structure keeps the weighted median current?
